idea.why: Two domain specialists working on independent sources in parallel, then a composer whose only job is presentation, then delivery. The Aggregate before each agent is a deliberate N-to-1 so the agent reasons over the whole batch once, which is the shape someone who has run this against a real inbox would pick.

structure.why: Almost all purpose-built types, no Code node reinventing anything, thirteen nodes proportionate. The weak point is the composer: rendering the HTML with a model every morning makes the presentation layer non-deterministic and unvalidated, and there is no guard stripping a stray fence before it reaches the mail body.

connections.why: The wiring states the real dependency graph rather than a convenient serialisation, with a real two-input Merge the composer depends on. Both fetchers carry alwaysOutputData with continueRegularOutput so an empty inbox still produces an item and the merge never starves.

answer.why: End to end what the brief asked for, with empty-state and anti-hallucination rules in both analyst prompts. What a reader might miss: the dashboard exists only inside an email, and nothing verifies the composer output is valid HTML before it is sent.

appraisal: The shape an experienced user would draw: parallel specialists over the two independent sources, structured parsers so the handoff is JSON rather than prose, one Merge where the streams genuinely rejoin, one model serving all three agents. Operational details show real thought rather than defaults. The soft spot is the presentation layer: the final HTML is generated by a model on every run, so layout drifts day to day, the cost is paid daily for output that barely changes, and a single stray fence renders as literal text with nothing in the graph to catch it. The first change is to move the HTML into a deterministic template fed by the two JSON payloads.
